question_text: This annual competition, held in the French capital since 1994, draws hundreds of entrants from across the Île-de-France region each year. The victor earns a cash prize of €4,000 among other things — and is subsequently barred from entering for the next four editions. The most recent winner is Sithamparappillai Jegatheepan of Fournil Didot, who claimed the top honour at the latest edition. Organised by the City of Paris and the Syndicat des Boulangers du Grand Paris, what is the name of this prestigious annual competition that crowns the best _______ maker in Paris?

Originating in Chinese mythology and later adopted across Japanese, Korean, and Vietnamese folklore, this creature is known by different names across cultures — Huli Jing, Kitsune, and Gumiho among them — yet shares a consistent set of traits wherever it appears: extraordinary age & shapeshifting ability. The number of ____ it possesses directly indicates the level of wisdom and magical power it has accumulated. It has toppled dynasties in Chinese legend, haunted imperial courts in Japanese folklore, and in modern pop culture lives on in beloved franchises such as Naruto, and in the Pokémon series, where it inspired the pokémon ____ . What is this mythical creature ?

This Stoke-on-Trent born sportsman, nicknamed "The Power," was one of the founding members of the company that brought his sport to global television audiences. After starting playing competitively at the age of 26, he dominated it for three decades, winning a record 16 World Championships, including eight consecutive titles between 1995 and 2002. He also holds the record for 11 televised ______, a difficult feat in the game, and was the first person to achieve two in the same match. Widely regarded as the greatest ever to play the sport, who is this legendary Englishman and what is the sport he called his own?

Developed in the 1960s by Norwegian toy manufacturer Asmund Laerdal in collaboration with anaesthesiologist Peter Safar, this medical training tool was designed to teach a certain newly standardised technique to the general public. Its female face was reportedly modelled on the death mask of an unidentified young woman pulled from the Seine in late 19th-century Paris. Decades later, it inadvertently lent its name to one of the most recognisable lines in pop culture. What is this ubiquitous training device (3 pts)? and what is the pop culture conenction?(7 pts)?

X is a literary fiction / thriller book by American author ML Rio about a group of Shakespeare conservatory students where they are witness to a crime which wreaks havoc on their lives. The title is borrowed from the Bard's "King Lear" where Edmund argues that human tendency to be ____ is not by necessity but by choice. The quote goes like this

"As _ _ __ ____ on necessity; fools by heavenly compulsion; knaves, thieves, and treachers by spherical pre-dominance; drunkards, liars, and adulterers by an enforc'd obedience of planetary influence"

Launched by a government actively engaged in an ongoing armed conflict, this digital platform was created to streamline the procurement of military and tactical supplies, allowing soldiers and units to request equipment directly and enabling donors from around the world to fund those requests transparently. Notably, it introduced a gamified element for frontline personnel — rewarding soldiers with points, badges, and rankings based on their battlefield contributions and equipment usage, turning the rigours of active combat into a structured incentive system. Its intuitive design drew inevitable comparisons to a certain global e-commerce giant, earning it a striking nickname that reflects both its function and the extraordinary circumstances under which it was born. Name the country that launched this platform (4 pts), and what is the platform called (6 pts)?

One of these two ancient symbols is associated with a Greek deity worshipped as the god of medicine and healing, and remains to this day the authentic emblem of the medical profession as recognised by the World Health Organisation. The other belongs to the messenger god of commerce and travellers, and has no historical connection to the healing arts whatsoever. Despite this clear distinction rooted in classical mythology, the two are routinely conflated in modern usage — particularly in the United States, where the latter has been widely and erroneously adopted by hospitals, medical institutions, and military medical corps, a mix-up many historians attribute to a clerical error made by the US Army Medical Corps in 1902 that quietly snowballed into widespread confusion. Name both symbols (5 pts each)?
answer_text: Rod of Asclepius; Caduceus of Hermes

question_text:
This American comedian and actor joined the cast of a long-running late-night sketch institution in 2013, where he became known for his uncanny celebrity impressions and a deadpan absurdist style that earned him a devoted following. After departing the show, he transitioned into film, landing a breakout dramatic role that surprised critics who had largely associated him with comedy — earning him widespread awards attention and cementing his reputation as a serious acting talent.

He is perhaps equally recognised today for his high-profile personal life, which has played out as publicly as any of his on-screen work. Name this performer (7 pts) and the show he rose to fame on (3 pts)?

This iconic American luxury house was founded in 1837 as a stationery and fancy goods store on Broadway, New York, with its first day of trading generating a mere $4.98 in sales — bankrolled by a modest thousand-dollar advance from the founder's father. Unlike its competitors at the time, it marked fixed prices on all goods, refused to allow haggling, and accepted only cash — no credit. It later pioneered America's first retail mail-order catalogue and revolutionised a certain important accessory as we know it today.

This small coastal town in the Netherlands, with a permanent population of just a few thousand, transforms each January into one of the most keenly watched destinations in the competitive world of a certain sport, drawing the planet's finest practitioners to a tournament that has been held annually since 1938. The event has long carried the name of a major industrial conglomerate with deep roots in India, which has served as its title sponsor for several decades. Past champions reads like a who's who of the all-time greats of the game, and an invitation to compete in its top tier is widely regarded as one of the most coveted in the sport. Name this small Dutch seaside town (6) and the competition(4).
answer_text: Wijk ann Zee; Tata Steel Chess

question_text: This controversial Marathi-language play, written by Pradeep Dalvi baseed on the book "may it please your honor" and first staged in 1997, presents its narrative entirely from the perspective of the man who carried out a one of the most historic crimes of 20th century. The production sparked immediate and fierce debate across Maharashtra and beyond, with authorities in several states moving to ban performances amid concerns that it glorified the perpetrator and offered a sympathetic platform to views many found deeply objectionable. Courts were drawn into the controversy on multiple occasions. Name this incendiary piece of Indian political theatre?

Connect(Exhaustive) and ID X:
• A collection of 116 pictures (one of which is for calibration) detailing but not limited to human life on Earth and the planet itself
• An eclectic 90-minute selection of music from many cultures, including Eastern and Western classics
• Sounds of earth containing various natural and artificial phenomena.
• Greetings in 55 languages
• Greetings from President Jimmy Carter and UN Secretary General Kurt Waldheim.
• X's brainwaves and heartbeats.
answer_text: Voyager Golden Record; Ann Druyan (Carl Sagan's Wife)

question_text: First observed informally in the 1960s in reference to the longevity of Broadway shows, and later formalised and popularised by the Lebanese-American statistician and essayist Nassim Nicholas Taleb in his writings on risk and uncertainty, this theory proposes a counterintuitive rule of thumb about the life expectancy of non-perishable things — ideas, technologies, institutions, and works of art. Its central claim is that the longer something has already survived, the longer it can be expected to continue to survive, meaning that a book in print for a century is likely to remain in print for another century, while a technology launched last year may be obsolete within months. Widely cited by investors, technologists, and philosophers when evaluating the durability of ideas and institutions, what is this principle named after a New York delicatessen?

Popularised by Andrew Hunt and David Thomas in their 1999 software engineering classic The Pragmatic Programmer, this widely practised and deceptively simple problem-solving technique requires a programmer stuck on a particularly stubborn piece of code to explain it aloud, line by line, to a completely silent and entirely unresponsive listener. The psychological mechanism behind its surprising effectiveness lies in the act of verbalisation itself — forcing the explainer to slow down, abandon assumptions, and articulate logic that had previously existed only as half-formed thought, frequently causing the error to reveal itself before the explanation is even complete. It has been adopted across disciplines as a general cognitive tool for untangling complex problems. The technique takes its name from the specific inanimate object that Hunt and Thomas whimsically suggested as the ideal listener. What is this debugging technique?

Born in the anarchic creative culture of early internet forums around 2008, this genre of crude, deliberately lo-fi digital illustration swept across the web in the early 2010s, built entirely around a cast of recurring faces — each representing a specific and universally recognisable human emotional state, from smug self-satisfaction to abject defeat. Characters such as "Forever Alone," "Me Gusta," and "Okay Guy" became shorthand for shared human experiences, making this one of the earliest examples of a visual language that transcended geographical and linguistic barriers entirely. Originally created and shared on a imageboard website using nothing more sophisticated than MS Paint, the format was later democratised by dedicated meme generators that allowed anyone to assemble their own strips — a feature that both accelerated its meteoric rise and, many argued, hastened its eventual decline into overexposure. What is this pioneering genre of internet humour (10 pts)?

Around 4.5–4.6 billion years ago, our planetary neighborhood was taking shape. A young star was forming at the center of a collapsing cloud of gas and dust. A broad ring of icy leftovers (X) was building up, while some individual icy fragments from this era would later appear in the inner solar system as a famous ____ (Y). What are X & Y?
answer_text: X: Kuiper Belt; Y: Halley's Comet
